High-quality input data is a critical requirement for clinical success in deep learning-based brain MRI segmentations. Although multiple methods to evaluate data quality exist, a primary concern remains whether a secondary, label-free labeling process can reliably identify low-quality scans. To examine this issue, we trained and assessed several deep learning models using datasets of varying sizes, comparing their performance against the established gold-standard protocol. Results demonstrated that small training cohorts performed significantly below expectations relative to larger datasets, indicating a generalization problem. Furthermore, we observed a strong dependency on specific site characteristics, suggesting a bias toward data from single centers. Consequently, we conclude that label-free labeling needs extensive multi-institutional training to achieve reliable accuracy.

Researchers have applied agent-based models to examine how meeting patterns emerge, focusing primarily on meeting selection rules and travel mode choices while validating theories using data from repeated in-person gatherings. However, this approach faces limitations due to the assumption of independent agent behaviors and an inability to model how a single agent's strategy evolves across varying meeting contexts. To address these issues and explore the emergence of multi-agent, multi-meeting structures, this study introduces a framework based on multi-agent recurrent meeting models. Key to this model is a random utility structure based on recurrent dynamics that incorporates both individual meeting specificities and a travel model rooted in differential accumulation rewards using travel time and distance. Comparison of theoretical predictions regarding meeting frequency and duration—derived from multi-agent simulations of cumulative agent preferences—demonstrates that the new model offers a more accurate fit for travel data than traditional independent agent methods. Furthermore, the model successfully identifies and validates the emergence of multi-agent meeting architectures, such as agent-only agglomerations and interlinked meeting schedules. Key outcomes include the detection of how differential travel reward accumulation shapes agent self-forming meetings and how it produces asymmetric patterns of self-organization along meeting complexity and duration. Finally, the research confirms that this new model effectively captures interdependent behaviors and strategy adaptation in recurrent meeting environments, demonstrating superior performance over prior theoretical expectations.

Achieving the most reliable values and uncertainty intervals for parton distribution function (PDF) parameters requires a theory framework that is explicitly integrated into global analyses of experimental and numerical data. While the modern Bayesian interpretation of PDF fitting has gained significant traction, it is by no means the sole required approach; a robust Bayesian setup demands prior distributions for both the PDF parameters and all confounding variables, regardless of whether these alternatives offer a fully consistent Bayesian solution. To address the latter rigorously, this paper introduces a novel theoretical Bayes factor formulation to quantify discrepancies between perturbative QCD evolution schemes, as well as updates from global analyses incorporating new datasets or theoretical advancements. Finally, we demonstrate and provide an operational code implementation for combining experimental data with such theoretical Bayes factors.

In on-policy reinforcement learning settings, newly sampled transitions are typically used to update the policy exclusively, gradually becoming outdated as more samples accumulate and prior data is discarded. While Experience Replay addresses this by preserving past samples to boost sample efficiency, it often requires significant storage; moreover, prioritized experience replay, which aims to optimize training by focusing on significant data, actually increases the variance of sample updates by heavily emphasizing outliers, thereby potentially hindering policy improvement. Instead of increasing the training variance, our approach, Variance Decrease-based Experience Replay (VDER), aims to reduce it within a limited memory context. By demonstrating that variance can be lowered through the refinement of the baseline while conserving memory, we propose the Linear-VDER algorithm to give greater weight to similar experiences without necessitating the complex structure of experience replay priority schemes. Additionally, VDER ensures retained samples remain relevant by confirming their utility for enhancing the subsequent policy, thus linking efficient data usage to policy improvement. Extensive experiments across multiple environments illustrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method.

Vertical Federated Learning (FED) has attracted significant interest from enterprises, allowing collaborative model training while keeping data within organizational boundaries. However, privacy concerns regarding vertical federated learning have rarely been examined from a user-centric angle. This work investigates the inherent vulnerabilities to privacy attacks posed by vertical federated learning operations. We examine the constraints of information separation that typically safeguard against attacks, contrasting various assault methodologies. We have developed a pioneering attack known as the Columnar Privacy Assault (CPL), which utilizes the inherent structural aspects of federated learning to launch attacks that are more precise and effective than those broadly targeted. Our findings indicate that, despite efforts to maintain privacy, vertical federated learning inherently exposes substantial risks of column-level privacy assaults. In specific industry-relevant scenarios involving federated classification, we demonstrated that the proposed CPL can accurately identify potential targets with an average precision of approximately ~93%, while also assessing the implications for both user confidentiality and the integrity of the learning models. Finally, we explored both the theoretical underpinnings and practical strategies for mitigating these risks through the column-level privacy assault approach.

Neural network architectures are rapidly evolving, with kernel networks recently gaining prominence by replacing activated dense layers to model non-linear patterns. These networks distinguish themselves with theoretical guarantees—such as interpolation capacities and generalization caps—derived from kernel theory that do not apply to standard deep networks. However, current estimates for the covariance operator usually assume stationarity and rely on random Fourier features, a rigid approach incapable of adapting to the specific data distribution at hand. This inflexibility leads to suboptimal kernel parameters when processing highly structured inputs like images, speech, or graphs, or when examining non-ergodic processes where traditional assumptions fail. Addressing these limitations, this paper introduces a novel estimator for the covariance operator computed directly from the dataset. By providing consistent estimates regardless of whether the process is ergodic, this method yields more rigorous generalization bounds and offers flexibility unattainable with prior random feature strategies. Extensive theoretical analysis accompanies robust numerical demonstrations comparing this data-dependent approach against existing methods.

Recently, the concept of "connectivity" was introduced to measure the non-randomness of a metal's electronic connectivity network. A strong negative connectivity (SCC) network emerged as this value drops below zero; such networks indicate that physical links preferentially form between adjacent nodes in a lattice rather than randomly. Using an effective field theory, we examine the consequences of SCC network topology on a square lattice. Our model successfully predicts a strongly non-random, SCC-driven metal with a linear spectral density at finite momenta, an outcome verifiable in future experiments via μSR techniques. Notably, the linear momentum dependence align in slope with that observed at k=(0,0), suggesting a potential new type of strongly correlated Dirac metal. This distinct phase stands in stark contrast to the widely discussed metallic percolative (network) states, which are characterised by Dirac bohemians at the gamma point with square dispersion that yields high-temperature superconductor symmetry. A subsequent section models various magnetic inducement scenarios, predicting magnetic inductive responses for links oriented along x and y directions as distinct linear slopes passing through momenta like (0, 0), (1/2 , 1/2 ), (1 , 0 ), etc., whose specific pattern should allow future μSR measurements to confirm this new strongly correlated metal classification.

Neutral heavy leptons are anticipated within many extensions to the Standard Model, particularly those involving extended gauge structures or large mixing angles; such leptons remain unconstrained by current data. To address this gap, we examine the NA62 experiment at CERN for signatures of massive neutral leptons in the specific $s$-channel process $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$. Our analysis reveals that assuming an unextended model, restricting the mass of these heavy neutral leptons below approximately 30 MeV allows the future generation of NA62 to severely limit their coupling, suppressing it significantly below existing bounds. This limitation applies irrespective of whether the mass spectrum stops at the neutrinoless point or the lighter seesaw scale, facilitating more sensitive searches in later stages. Additionally, we outline an alternative theoretical framework where neutral leptons become barely complex—either due to neutrless states or non-negligible mixing ratios—and discuss the implications for future searches.

Our analysis reveals a parameter regime where the spectral index deviation reaches $10^{-2}$—matching current observational constraints—while the scalar field variance attains $20\overline{}$, indicating BHs. These results suggest that Primordial Black holes form during this phase, with such objects becoming an essential element post-inflationary epoch, providing a potential solution regarding supermassive black hole origins.

In the context of crucial votes, erroneous counting techniques introduce significant vulnerabilities. This paper introduces iOCR, a novel method that integrates Optical Character Recognition (OCR) with logical constraints to extract data from election tabulation screens, effectively correcting common errors. While standard OCRC often struggles with the visual complexity of election interfaces, our approach employs recognition post-processing that applies external knowledge to refine and correct raw outputs. We evaluated our system on a dataset of 1,300 images captured from 435 election sessions drawn to and from different geographic areas and varying screen sizes. Our results indicate that iOCR achieves an 99.9% accuracy, significantly surpassing 98.8% accuracy provided by state of the art OCRC, demonstrating not only the superiority of our method but highlighting potential introductions of vote theft risks.

Temporal models are widely utilized to capture evolving patterns across various domains, with optimal performance typically achieved by auto-regressive (AR) structures. Although previous research demonstrated that standard temporal regression achieves consistent estimation despite over-parameterization, this paper addresses the scenarios involving very large over-parameterization and extensive noise levels. We demonstrate that the full range of parameters fitted within a regularized over-parameterized temporal model—including those unrelated to the true underlying structure—become benignly overfitted. Specifically, using an auto-regressive model of order $p$ as an illustrative case, we show two key contributions: first, the complete parameter vector, not just the intercept and slope parameters, yields predictions consistent with those of the true minimal model; second, the model exhibits approximate symmetry around a central point in time, a unique occurrence in statistical estimation problems.

In decentralized storage networks, efficient and reliable pricing strategies are vital. These strategies typically rely on a significant portion of data owners' contributions to achieve optimal outcomes, which benefits both the planning agent and future planners with limited experience or access. However, purely statistical approaches may yield inefficient results when facing diverse groups of data owners, particularly in scenarios limited by small sample sizes. To address this paper introduces Cautious Self-Planning (CS), an adaptive method utilizing bilateral planning contracts to generate future revenue for storage deployment. The CS algorithm proceeds in stages, beginning with the strategic pricing of existing capacities and continuing with the careful cautious acquisition of additional storage. Each data provider independently decides whether to sell their capacity and at what price point, making these choices the central focus of both capacity planning sessions. Capacity self-planning offers a significant advantage over statistical methods in producing high expected planning results characterised by high income generation and adequate storage levels. Both numerical experiments and extensive simulations substantiate these observations.

We analyze the quantum transport of two-band HgTe gapless quantum wells containing Dirac particles, focusing on the interplay between well parameters and impurity scattering. Our study involves calculating the conduction characteristics via the Landauer-Büttiker formalism within the Born approximation, explicitly addressing various impurity potentials and scattering ranges to determine their impact on quantum conductance. Our findings reveal that in a central region of the well, Conductor behaves as a diffusive system where conductance fluctuates due to coherent scattering off impurities. These fluctuations are highly sensitive to the potential shape, impurity range, and potential strength. Furthermore, we observe significant conductance modulation caused by altering the quantum wells' parameters. Consequently, we suggest manipulating these conductive properties through modifications of the impurity potentials and well configurations.

This study proposes a new in-band Game-Theoretic (GT) method for allocating radio resource blocks (RBs) in Dynamic Time Division Duplexing (TDD) networks. As a non-cooperative game, the model addresses resource allocation challenges where base stations act as players, available RBs are strategies, and achievable data rates serve as the utility function. The solution concept is the Nash Equilibrium (NE), and the suggested algorithm ensures convergence to an NE state. While the framework operates in dynamic environments with varying traffic loads and resource availability, it distinguishes itself by determining allocation decisions independently and without negotiation between base stations. The proposed data-rate calculation considers both physical layer constraints and scheduling limitations. In simulations, the method's efficacy is validated against other dynamic TDD algorithms and non-game-theoretic approaches, demonstrating significant gains in spectral efficiency and latency reduction. These results confirm the framework's potential for effective resource management in Dynamic TDD settings.

This study investigates whether the ability of Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNN) to exactly solve contrastive dynamics implies it can also solve gradient-based flow. The analysis provides a negative answer for general Hamiltonians but confirms a positive result for quadratic Hamiltonians, which are inherently gradient-based. Consequently, any contrastive task solvable by Hamiltonian layers can be reformed into a gradient-descent dynamics task while preserving continuous symmetry. As these symmetries permit continuous reconstruction of data points from their trajectories, such reconstruction enables a novel estimation method known as contrastive dynamics-based differentiation (CD-diff).

Enhancing the reliability of ML systems is crucial, with trust ratings serving as a primary mechanism for users to express their confidence in automated predictions. Building on this insight, the author introduced the DAMA framework, which operates on a multi-agent architecture where each agent trains on a subset of the dataset. Framework uses damads to calculate a subset-specific aggregate trust metric to weight training data; consequently, more agents facilitate better data partitioning and calculation of the subset-specific damad, leading to more homogeneous subsets. Furthermore, DAMADS proposes two novel, multi-agent frameworks: human collaboration enables agents to communicate about subsets to refine homogeneity, while independent agent operation allows each to improve individual model reliability. Both approaches leverage the consensus of multiple streams to enhance overall trust and system performance.

Ultimately, this research sets a foundation for developing advanced semiconductor devices grounded in multi-quasiparticle dynamics.

Grain Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as a prominent tool for processing and analyzing graphs. However, theoretical foundations regarding the theoretical undercurrents behind GNN advantages on general graph-structured data remain challenging. This paper serves as accessible introduction to the theoretical undercurrents of GNN advantages and explores bounds for dynamic system behavior. Specifically, we present a refined bound on the diffusion process, improving upon prior work by restricting the mixing time requirement from stationary distribution convergence to basic confinement within a subset of nodes. We also introduce an innovative approach to modeling and analyzing complex system dynamics, identifying critical thresholds and phase transitions. Furthermore, we clarify framework conditions links between critical phenomena and node initial configurations or interactions. We discuss implications within statistical physics, social dynamics, and epidemiology to illustrate how advanced GNN methods can enhance system analysis despite these developing challenges remain significant areas of growth in interpreting dynamic patterns.

Lesions in the brain disrupt normal neural structures, posing a significant challenge for the development of robust neural networks. To address this issue, we introduced a cerebral adversarial lesion generation model (Brain-ALGM), designed with a feedback mechanism that guides search directions using classification errors to efficiently generate disruptive brain faults. Although effective, dependency on multiple training runs of a pre-existing model within this framework can substantially extend training periods. Extending this concept, we developed the Cerebral Adversarial Progressive Lesion Auto-Encoder (CAPPALGM) by replacing the base encoder-decoder structure of the initial model with an Adverse Variational Auto-Encoder framework. This upgrade enables the generation of realistic brain scans across varying resolutions and augments the model's capacity to capture complex spatial dependencies through an end-to-end training regimen. Both CAPPALGM and ALGM were evaluated through extensive experiments; both demonstrated superiority over current state-of-the-axis encoders and confounders in four critical dimensions: the authenticity and distributional similarity of generated data, the capability for image reconstruction, and the classification accuracy of downstream tasks. Notably, CAPPALGM achieved a substantial reduction in training time relative to the Adverse Guided Model with which it was compared.

GP 2 was the first programming language capable of fundamentally changing its own parser, extending from a standard configuration all the way up to a fully object-oriented model. Because the configuration is so flexible, the sequence with which statements execute becomes absolutely critical for optimization. This paper presents GP 2 Enhancements in Compiler Work (GP 2:CC), an optimizer tailored specifically for GP 2's unique orientation. We outline the GP 2 configuration language and analyze why traditional data-flow optimization methods fall short in this environment. The proposed solver addresses this by determining the most efficient linearization of statements using a graph-based approach, considering both semantic operations and cost. The results demonstrate a reduction in execution times of up to four orders of magnitude compared to the standard compiler.

Star normal quotient diagrams serve as an efficient graphical representation of isomorphism graphs for finite groups, with their construction and drawing traditionally relying on the construction of normal quotient diagrams first. However, to facilitate visualization, often a set of diagrams containing only cycles needs to be generated from the initial construction. In this work, we define an innovative infinite family of diagrams containing open paths alongside cycles. We demonstrate that these innovative diagrams maintain validity for visualization purposes by adopting the designation "twisted wreath structure." To date, this collection constitutes the only available realization of "twisted" or "opened" structures within the framework of normal quotient diagrams.

Model selection or sparse estimation for categorical variables remains challenging, despite extensive research on continuous and categorical outcomes, though significant progress has been made on both. We examine a high-dimensional setting, offering an innovative penalty that combines flexibility with rigorous theoretical guarantees, while easily accommodating various estimation techniques. Our method enhances the standard Group Lasso framework, which suits categorical variables less effectively. Despite its strength, Standard Group Lasso suffers from three key drawbacks: (i) unnecessary model complexity, (ii) potential biased parameter estimates, (iii) and biased inference regarding variable significance testing, which we address through enhanced design. Comprehensive numerical simulations and an analytical case study utilizing over 30,000 genes and more than 7,000 binary factors demonstrate performance superiority on multiple tasks, including variable selection accuracy and inference quality relative to existing group-level approaches for categorical contexts, confirming that (enhanced) Group Lasso yields sparse solutions even when competing with correct selection or sparse estimators, though perhaps not always optimal in terms.

Rendering point, line, and face elements from vector map data while maintaining data fidelity presents significant challenges. Although commercial solutions exist, effective anti-aliasing techniques for calculating map road junctions remain underdeveloped, frequently resulting in distorted junctions that impair user experience and undermine the rendering's authenticity and visual appeal. Considering the primary functions of online mapping platforms and the mature hardware capabilities of graphical cards, this paper proposes a novel spatial anti-aliasing algorithm tailored for road map intersections. By leveraging the screen space properties of triangular meshes, the method calculates sub-pixel occupancy rates to perform weighted color blending, thereby achieving high-quality anti-aliasing effects. Experimental validation, comparing this approach against traditional anti-aliasing protocols within a real mapping system, confirms that the proposed algorithm significantly enhances rendering quality at map road intersections.

Recently, source separation techniques using convolution-recurrent neural networks have gained significant attention, initially introduced to enhance performance in tone language environments like Chinese through the SEPRSN framework. Building upon this concept, we introduce a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN). This model operates in a single estimation stage to simultaneously process short-term long short-term time context (LS-TMC) and long-term frequency domain characteristics (LS-FMC). Specifically, the network leverages convolutional units along BiLSTM modules within its branch structures to respectively capture these complementary features. Evaluations conducted in noisy conditions demonstrate that DPCRN consistently outperforms existing primary methods across three key metrics: intelligent speech quality assessments, objective noise reduction rates, and listening quality subjectively reviewed by humans.

Non-linear charged anti-de Sitter (AdS) black holes exhibit a specific temperature at which phase transitions occur, causing the characteristic temperature plateau of the greybody factor to disappear entirely. Because the plateaus are absent, the corresponding extremal event horizon exhibits dynamics that preclude the formation of an event horizon during radiation; consequently, these black holes radiate toward an extremal non-zero temperature non-black state rather than settling at an extremal zero temperature. Furthermore, the variation of the entropy for these non-linear charged systems does not follow the proportionality required by the standard shadow thermodynamic principle. This deviation indicates that the conventional definition of this principle must be extended when applied to non-linear charged systems with non-zero extremal temperature plateaus.

The focus of this paper is upon the entangled coherent states (ECS), demonstrating various image-based phase-space distribution functions known as tomograms, while examining their key intrinsic traits. Our analysis reveals that the resultant decoherence manifests clearly within these tomograms, appearing much like a conventional ensemble where ECS characteristics are lost; nevertheless, some form of synchronization between modes emerges and is also visible in the data. Furthermore, we observe that mathematical expressions typically associated with ECS features, such as interference effects and ECS variance, not only remain valid within the quantum tomogram framework but accurately depict the specific changes or discrepancies this classical-like interpretation entails.

This study analyzes the behavior of decoupling techniques applied to problems with constrained options. We focus on the situation where an agent gradually reduces their previous policy's recommendations, taking their initial strategy being probability-independent. We demonstrate that, within a specific neighborhood of the start, the typical decrease in the optimization value follows a precise mathematical form. This form includes a coefficient that depends on how the agent adjusts policies and divides by the square root of the episode count, effectively mirating standard statistical error terms. The dependence on adjustment choices is compared and estimated, with these results connected to earlier work in OLS regression and combinatorial topics like decoupled Euler-Lagrange equations.

Combining ferromagnets with photonic crystals can significantly alter the propagation properties of light while simultaneously providing information about interacting magnetic states. Nevertheless, the propagation symmetry of surfaces within conventional magnetophotonic crystals remains invariant regardless of magnetization direction, limiting their utility for non-reciprocal mirror imaging and other applications that require magnetization sensitivity. Although engineering anisotropic surface propagation has previously been documented, these approaches typically demand the incorporation of bulk photonic elements into multilayered designs, complicating both fabrication and optical access. In this work, we demonstrate that a single-layer surface magnetophotonic lattice achieves propagation symmetry breaking induced specifically by the ferromagnetic state, with a total thickness of only 0.5 wavelengths. By utilizing a simple geometric arrangement of magnetic-tunneling resonance bars oriented at 45 degrees, we realize the first magnetization-oriented magnetic-photonic lattice confined to an interface layer. Our analysis via Hopcard-Kretzschmar (HK) RPA theory matches experimental verification obtained through time-domain reflectometry (TDR) and far-field microscopy, and we attribute the resulting anisotropy to the coupling between the saturation magnetic state and the calculated group velocity patterns of surface electromagnetic modes.

Decision-based white-space attack (DABA) represents a significant advancement, enabling effective black-box image attacks while supporting multi-object and zero-transfer scenarios. Assuming full access to a decision function, these attacks however, require distinct training datasets for each specific target network. Since collecting labeled datasets for every new model is often impr feasible, we address a critical limitation: the inability to transfer knowledge to a new network without accessible training data. We introduce a methodology that achieves this transfer by leveraging decision values from a source network as training data for new black-box targets, utilizing model insights generated by an image differentiation attack. Verification within a ResNet image classification context demonstrates significant successes; specifically, we observe average accuracy drops across three different black-box image attacks compared to non-transfer methods, and we identify that this approach also significantly degrades the performance of state-of-the-art differential privacy attacks.

Social interaction is essential to human existence, with research indicating that a significant portion of our knowledge is acquired through observing others. While recent Self-Observation Learning models have shown promise, Co-Observation Learning presents a distinct advantage: it allows agents to acquire multiple skill types not by imitation, but by monitoring both peer actions and environmental changes, offering a more realistic framework than assuming an unlimitd expert agent. However, existing methods for Co-Observation Learning still depend on having a virtual (virtual) agent in the setup. We introduce Co-OP, which enables co-observation reinforcement learning exclusively with an interaction between two intelligent agents, without requiring agents to look at an virtual. Our proposed Co-OP allows an agent, starting from random actions, to extract shared patterns from the actions of another learning agent. Experiments demonstrate that Co-OP outperforms current methods in sample efficiency and exhibits significant advantages in transfer learning and without the the agent effect.

This study examines algorithm performance within high-capacity natural language generation systems, specifically analyzing the Reinforce algorithm across various generation task sizes. We introduce the HyperTuning approach to mitigate the bias typically associated with maximum likelihood training used in baseline selection. Evaluations conducted on text generation tasks demonstrate that HyperTuning achieves significant bias reduction and surpasses standard baselines on neural machine translation tasks featuring moderate to large action space complexities, although the proposed method does introduce increased inference overhead.

We present and analyze a experimental non-equilibrium steady state arising from the periodic modulation of a qubit's coupling to a thermal bath at temperature $T$. Using process tomography, we determine the qubit's dynamic density matrix, revealing that despite the driving, the system reaches a unique non-equilibrium steady state decoupled from the drive frequency. As the temperature drops, both experimental results and theoretical analysis show a clear transition from a mixed quantum state to a pure state. Furthermore, the transition point shifts when altering the heating rate or driving frequency, and hysteresis appears under certain conditions, all of which align with predictions. The mechanism is attributed to the emergence of an effective anti-periodic behavior, as the heating induces an apparent unitary evolution.

MongoDB is widely recognized as a dominant, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database; however, initial releases were criticized for the lack of strict transaction support. Although full transactions were introduced subsequently, current evidence suggests implementations may fail to uphold transactional integrity, a critical component even for databases that claim to support distributed transactions with linearizability. To address this, we present MongoDBTx, a systematic framework designed to verify the integrity of transactions within MongoDB. By combining a customized, distributed simulation environment with an adaptable verification algorithm tailored to specific protocols, MongoDBTx aims to expose real-world breaches that standard testing methods often miss, utilizing verified algorithms like those by Cochrane et al. (2017) as a foundation. In executing our evaluations, we utilized this setup to validate the versions 4.0 through 4.4 of MongoDB, uncovering and fixing a linearizability breach in 4.0, and subsequently confirming that 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4 maintain both the asserted linearizability and overall transaction integrity. Our findings provide essential validation for the operational correctness of widespread distributed transactions in MongoDB.

We examine the dynamics of particle localization within nano-scale assemblies containing 14 to 142 particles, where interatomic forces are either local and local plus non-local, governed by Lennard-Jones potentials. Because these interactions lack sufficient constraints to determine particle positions uniquely, the system exhibits complex, non-trivial geometry and mechanics. We analyze these structures by applying matrix formulations of Newton's equations of motion and use phase space analysis—specifically plotting potential energy against matrix determinant values—to reveal the design principles behind different network behaviors. Our findings indicate that nano-assemblies combining local and non-local triangular interactions can exist in discrete states characterized by complex spatial arrangements that are mathem akin to those generated by quasicrystalline tilings.

The concept of solar breeze, first introduced by Nelson and Sonett in 1973 based on interplanetary magnetic field measurements from Mariner 5, divides the interplanetary medium into an inner zone characterized by orderly, radial field lines and an outer zone, known as the heliospheric current sheet region. This division is defined not by latitude, but by thermal properties: inner and outer regions are identified as the inner solar breeze (ISB) and outer solar breeze (OSB), respectively, with the separation boundary located where the perpendicular heating balance between perpendicular heat gain ($Q_{\perp}$) and plasma heat storage ($E_{\text{th}}\times N$) is equal. While classical beliefs suggested the ISB/OSB boundary resided near 0.3 and 0.5 astronomical units (AU)—implying only the inner solar breeze should have been encountered within the first 0.4 AU of the inner heliosphere—Parker Solar Probe (PSS) surprisingly detected both ISB and OSB conditions at much closer distances before its perihelion passage at 0.3 AU. The discovery of pervasive outer solar breeze features so close to the Sun challenges established heating models, as current mechanisms like radial thermal conduction and standard algebraic processes prove inadequate, thereby underscoring an urgent requirement for new theoretical frameworks to explain these enigmatic plasma heating dynamics.

Speech-emotion recognition (SER) faces the cross-domain problem, in which performance drops significantly when deployed in new environments despite achieving high accuracy within the same domain. Differences in dataset distribution are a primary cause of this failure; however, current cross-domain methods predominantly compare disparate subtasks—such as sentiment polarity versus specific emotional categories—neglecting the distributions of individual emotion labels (e.g., how "joy" appears in one domain versus another). This paper re-examines the cross-domain challenge with a focus on specific emotion labels and addresses the domain shift through domain adaptation, adopting a Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework for SER to better handle the inherent sequential nature of emotion classification. The proposed D3RL approach starts with an off-the-shelf RL-based SER baseline. It assumes a source domain with sufficient training data and multiple target domains, each containing sparse data. To mitigate target-domain bias caused by sparse samples, D3RL generates synthetic data by sampling from a learned mixture model. Furthermore, D3RL adapts the collected RL-trained agent with transfer learning techniques to accommodate further target-domain variations. In wide-ranging experiments covering diverse domains and emotional taxonomies, we demonstrate that D3RL substantially improves performance and significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art cross-domain methods.

This paper examines a differential equation generalized from the standard Hermite form, characterizing its series solutions and establishing a connection between these general solutions and Hermite polynomials. We explicitly construct monodromy-free solutions valid across the entire complex plane and analyze the uniqueness conditions for such solutions. By extending the superintegrable nature of the Hermian system to this broader class, we achieve the calculation of generalized constants of the motion unique to each series solution component. This constant ensures that all solutions can be expressed as linear combinations of super-eigenstates. In realistic dynamic models where individuals progress through distinct stages, real-world networks usually give prior beneficiaries access to resources, creating initial disparities. Our analysis compares two frameworks: the first assigns top-tier connections stochastically to initially favored groups, while the second optimizes these connections deterministically to maximize the resource's ubiquity across generations. Finally, we test the robustness of these results against variations in network formation parameters.

Brightness scans represent a fundamental technique in beam diagnostics, serving as a primary tool for characterizing charged particle beams and fields generated by neutral beams. This paper examines a quantized, distributed optimization framework operating under malicious attacks. Within this model, at least one adversary introduces errors into communication data with the goal of preventing consensus among agents, while those agents strive to reach consensus despite such disruptions. Assuming the target function is convex and differentiable, and that the communication network forms a connected graph, we employ subgradient methods to solve the problem. We formulate and analyze the case where the attacker acts maliciously but honestly: data remains altered, yet the agent simply forwards the received information without verifying its integrity. Our results demonstrate that subgradient optimization enables agents to converge to a near-optimal solution with minimal final deviation, even when an agent faces an arbitrary malicious but honest adversary who knows the algorithm and graph topology. Final discrepancies are driven by factors including step size selection, communication noise intensity, and the magnitude of the attack. We support our findings with simulations to validate the proposed theory.

Outlier detection, influence functions, and sensitivity analysis share a common basis in integrating statistical learning with dynamical systems theory, though these approaches often utilize different data sets or theoretical frameworks. In this work, we unify these methods by introducing a new concept: data-guided influence values (DGI). We demonstrate the application of DGI for both clustering and detecting events, highlighting how these strategies perform even when the system's underlying equations remain unknown (i.e., "data-hammy"). Since the proposed approach requires minimal system knowledge, comparing it to traditional techniques that depend on precise equation identification becomes challenging; consequently, we show through simulation studies that Data-Guided Influence Values effectively enhance performance across these scenarios. Achieving autonomous navigation for marine robots requires accurately perceiving and adapting to environmental changes, a capability that is frequently disrupted by noise and significantly impacted by temporal fluctuations. Standard Bayesian optimization methods, which rely on Gaussian processes (GPs) to learn navigation, often fail in this domain because they cannot effectively capture and respond to how noise levels and robot trajectories change over time. To resolve this, we introduce a framework called Temporal Variation Learning with Sparse GP (TV-SGP). This approach jointly learns the optimal robot navigation paths and models the statistical shifts in environment dynamics. Specifically, the model accounts for shifts in mean values and covariance structures caused by progressing times and different routes. By utilizing an unsupervised learning paradigm where both model parameters and TV-SGP hyperparameters are learned from sensor data to maximize posterior probability, the system discovers how the marine environment evolves with time and path selection. The resulting model is both computationally efficient and scalable. Extensive simulations using realistic underwater sensors and comparative tests validate the proposed method, demonstrating its superiority over current state-of-the-art temporal variation learning techniques for robot navigation tasks.

Our analysis reveals that EE T Tauri stars are segmented by scale: most operate in the regime where the magnetosphere-disk interaction dominates fluctuation behavior, while those larger than approximately 0.3 R$_\odot$ (including XX Cha and L Pyx) function in a regime where accretion is regulated by disk physics. Notably, XX Cha represents a unique case where accretion varies over more than an order of magnitude; as this star ages and its magnetosphere retreats, PET cycles shorten, and we project similar strong fluctuations will occur when the magnetosphere becomes too weak to constrain the disk entirely. The integration of wind and photovoltaic generators offers a sustainable solution to mitigate climate change; however, these sources lack the ability to maintain grid frequency within its standard range. These findings suggest that policy mandates determining absolute minimum thresholds for FRR, 15-minute Secondary Control (SC), 1-second Secondary Control (SCC/SCS), and Primary Frequency Response (PFR) should be revised to adopt dynamic quota mechanisms capable of adapting across different market jurisdictions.

A significant obstacle in modeling angular data lies in constructing accurate and computationally feasible models of dependencies among directions. To overcome this, Bausch, Kowalski, and Vasil'evov introduced the spherical random field (SRF), defined by the property that the marginal distribution of any node $j$ on the sphere depends solely on the field realizations of its neighbors. They initially demonstrated via Monte Carlo simulations that one-step recurrences—methods requiring the marginal of node $i$ to rely exclusively on the conditional distributions of neighboring nodes given all other fields—successfully capture correlations within this particular SRF. However, standard Monte Carlo techniques often fail to provide sufficient accuracy for such estimations. In this paper, we present and evaluate the spherical harmonic expansion method as a precise alternative for deriving these one-step recurrences. Numerical experiments comparing our approach with simulations demonstrate that the spherical harmonic expansion yields markedly more precise and reliable estimates.

Dysfunctional nuclei associated with diseases can often be detected by examining their morphology, making the task of nuclear segmentation a prevalent step in analysis regarding cell populations; however, traditional automated nuclei segmentation techniques tend to yield suboptimal results when dealing with complex and varied pathological patterns. Furthermore, since evaluating cell morphology is critical for diagnosing diseases like cancer, any error in segmentation directly compromises diagnostic accuracy. To address these issues, we introduce W-Nucleus Net (W-Net), a multi-stage nuclear segmentation network tailored for pathological histology. Experiments utilizing external pseudo-ground truths to exclude segementation errors demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, analyses of incorrectly segmented cases in the result set support the validity of this two-phase architecture.
